TERMINATION OF PARENTAL RIGHTS (FREEDOM FROM PARENTAL CUSTODY AND CONTROL) — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Jordan Lee · Pat Morgan

ABOUT THIS INFORMATION SHEET
This information sheet describes California's "Freedom from Parental Custody and Control" proceeding under Family Code Part 4 (commencing with Section 7800) — the statutory action by which a court may declare a child free from the custody and control of a parent, terminating that parent's rights. It summarizes the recognized statutory grounds, the standard of proof, who may petition, notice and counsel procedures, and the effect of a resulting judgment as reflected in the current Family Code. This document concerns the interested-person action brought under Family Code Part 4; it does not summarize the separate termination process that occurs inside a juvenile dependency case, and it does not itself prepare, file, or serve a petition on behalf of Jordan Lee regarding Alex Lee. This is not a substitute for consulting a licensed attorney.

PURPOSE OF THE PROCEEDING AND LEGAL EFFECT OF A JUDGMENT
Family Code section 7802 authorizes a proceeding under Part 4 "for the purpose of having a minor child declared free from the custody and control of either or both parents." Family Code section 7803 states the consequence of a resulting declaration: it "terminates all parental rights and responsibilities with regard to the child." These are two separate sections within the same Part 4 general-provisions chapter — section 7802 states the proceeding's purpose while section 7803 states its ultimate legal effect — and neither restates or independently confirms the other's text.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "A proceeding may be brought under this part for the purpose of having a minor child declared free from the custody and control of either or both parents."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 7802, Fam. Code § 7802 (West, current through 2025 legislation) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=7802.)
  "A declaration of freedom from parental custody and control pursuant to this part terminates all parental rights and responsibilities with regard to the child."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 7803, Fam. Code § 7803 (West, current through 2025 legislation) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=7803.)
  Known gap: Section 7803 states that a declaration terminates parental rights and responsibilities, but neither section addresses what happens to the child's custody or legal status after termination (for example, whether an adoption follows), nor whether a later Probate Code guardianship or a separate adoption proceeding is required to establish a new legal parent. This document does not address the juvenile dependency system's parallel termination process under Welfare and Institutions Code section 366.26, which involves a different petitioning party (the county agency), a different procedural posture, and different governing standards than the Family Code Part 4 action described here.

CLEAR AND CONVINCING EVIDENCE STANDARD
Family Code section 7821 states that "a finding pursuant to this chapter shall be supported by clear and convincing evidence, except as otherwise provided." This heightened standard governs the findings on the statutory grounds set out in Chapter 2 of Part 4 (the grounds described elsewhere in this document, including abandonment, neglect or dependency-based deprivation, felony conviction, and mental disability).

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "A finding pursuant to this chapter shall be supported by clear and convincing evidence, except as otherwise provided."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 7821, Fam. Code § 7821 (West, current through 2025 legislation) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=7821.)
  Known gap: Section 7821 by its terms applies to findings "pursuant to this chapter" — Chapter 2's grounds provisions — and its own text notes an exception ("except as otherwise provided") that this clause does not enumerate. Other procedural findings within Part 4 carry their own, separately stated clear-and-convincing requirements (for example, a finding supporting in-chambers child testimony under section 7892, addressed elsewhere in this document); this section does not itself establish the standard applicable to every finding made in the proceeding.

STATUTORY GROUND: ABANDONMENT
Family Code section 7822(a) permits a proceeding where, among other listed circumstances, "the child has been left without provision for the child's identification by the child's parent or parents" or has been left in another's care and custody for six months (or, under a related provision, by one parent in the other parent's care for one year) "without any provision for the child's support, or without communication from the parent or parents, with the intent on the part of the parent or parents to abandon the child." Subdivision (b) provides that "the failure to provide identification, failure to provide support, or failure to communicate is presumptive evidence of the intent to abandon," and that if the parent has made "only token efforts to support or communicate with the child, the court may declare the child abandoned."

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "(a) A proceeding under this part may be brought if any of the following occur: (1) The child has been left without provision for the child’s identification by the child’s parent or parents. (2) The child has been left by both parents or the sole parent in the care and custody of another person for a period of six months without any provision for the child’s support, or without communication from the parent or parents, with the intent on the part of the parent or parents to abandon the child."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 7822(a), Fam. Code § 7822, subd. (a) (West, current through 2025 legislation) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=7822.)
  "The failure to provide identification, failure to provide support, or failure to communicate is presumptive evidence of the intent to abandon. If the parent or parents have made only token efforts to support or communicate with the child, the court may declare the child abandoned by the parent or parents."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 7822(b), Fam. Code § 7822, subd. (b) (West, current through 2025 legislation) — quoted alongside subdivision (a) of the same section 7822; not an independent source from it (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=7822.)
  Known gap: The statute does not define "token efforts" numerically or by any bright-line test; whether a given level of contact or support crosses that threshold is left to case-by-case determination that this document does not resolve. Section 7822 also contains a separate publication-notice pathway, for a child left without identification and parents of unknown whereabouts, that this clause does not summarize in full.

STATUTORY GROUND: NEGLECT, CRUEL TREATMENT, OR PROLONGED DEPENDENCY
Family Code section 7823(a) permits a proceeding, on satisfaction of all its listed requirements, where "the child has been neglected or cruelly treated by either or both parents" — a finding of severe sexual abuse under a cross-referenced Welfare and Institutions Code provision serves as prima facie evidence of this — or where "the child has been a dependent child of the juvenile court under any subdivision of Section 300 of the Welfare and Institutions Code and the parent or parents have been deprived of the child's custody for one year before the filing of a petition pursuant to this part."

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "(1) The child has been neglected or cruelly treated by either or both parents. A finding that a parent committed severe sexual abuse, as described in paragraph (6) of subdivision (b) of Section 361.5 of the Welfare and Institutions Code, against the child shall be prima facie evidence that the parent has neglected or cruelly treated the child within the meaning of this subdivision. (2) The child has been a dependent child of the juvenile court under any subdivision of Section 300 of the Welfare and Institutions Code and the parent or parents have been deprived of the child’s custody for one year before the filing of a petition pursuant to this part."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 7823(a), Fam. Code § 7823, subd. (a) (West, current through 2025 legislation) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=7823.)
  Known gap: This ground incorporates the juvenile dependency system's jurisdictional finding under Welfare and Institutions Code section 300, but this document does not itself state that section's criteria for dependency jurisdiction, which are governed by a different code with its own procedures. The statute also provides that physical custody "for insubstantial periods of time" does not interrupt the one-year clock, a fact-specific determination this clause does not further quantify.

STATUTORY GROUND: FELONY CONVICTION PROVING UNFITNESS, AND CONCEPTION BY RAPE
Family Code section 7825(a) permits a proceeding where "the child is one whose parent or parents are convicted of a felony" and "the facts of the crime of which the parent or parents were convicted are of such a nature so as to prove the unfitness of the parent or parents to have the future custody and control of the child." A separate subdivision (b) permits a mother to bring a proceeding against a father "where the child was conceived as a result of an act in violation of Section 261 of the Penal Code, and where the father was convicted of that violation," in which circumstance "there is a conclusive presumption that the father is unfit to have custody or control of the child."

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "(1) The child is one whose parent or parents are convicted of a felony. (2) The facts of the crime of which the parent or parents were convicted are of such a nature so as to prove the unfitness of the parent or parents to have the future custody and control of the child."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 7825(a), Fam. Code § 7825, subd. (a) (West, current through 2025 legislation) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=7825.)
  "The mother of a child may bring a proceeding under this part against the father of the child, where the child was conceived as a result of an act in violation of Section 261 of the Penal Code, and where the father was convicted of that violation. For purposes of this subdivision, there is a conclusive presumption that the father is unfit to have custody or control of the child."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 7825(b), Fam. Code § 7825, subd. (b) (West, current through 2025 legislation) — quoted alongside subdivision (a) of the same section 7825; not an independent source from it (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=7825.)
  Known gap: The felony ground in subdivision (a) is not automatic upon any felony conviction — the statute requires the court to find that the facts of the particular crime prove unfitness for future custody, a case-by-case determination this document does not resolve. The conclusive presumption in subdivision (b) applies only to the narrow class of cases involving a Penal Code section 261 conviction resulting in the child's conception; it does not extend to convictions for other sex offenses.

STATUTORY GROUND: PARENTAL MENTAL DISABILITY, AND ITS EVIDENTIARY AND COUNSEL REQUIREMENTS
Family Code section 7827 defines "mentally disabled," for purposes of this ground, to mean "that a parent or parents suffer a mental incapacity or disorder that renders the parent or parents unable to care for and control the child adequately," and permits a proceeding where the parent is mentally disabled and likely to remain so in the foreseeable future. Except as the statute otherwise provides for out-of-state parents, a finding under this ground requires "the evidence of any two experts, each of whom shall be a physician and surgeon, certified either by the American Board of Psychiatry and Neurology or under Section 6750 of the Welfare and Institutions Code, a licensed psychologist who has a doctoral degree in psychology and at least five years of postgraduate experience in the diagnosis and treatment of emotional and mental disorders." Separately, if the parent facing termination under this section lacks an attorney, "the court shall appoint an attorney for the parent pursuant to Article 4 (commencing with Section 7860) of Chapter 3, whether or not a request for the appointment is made by the parent."

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "“Mentally disabled” as used in this section means that a parent or parents suffer a mental incapacity or disorder that renders the parent or parents unable to care for and control the child adequately."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 7827(a), Fam. Code § 7827, subd. (a) (West, current through 2025 legislation) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=7827.)
  "the evidence of any two experts, each of whom shall be a physician and surgeon, certified either by the American Board of Psychiatry and Neurology or under Section 6750 of the Welfare and Institutions Code, a licensed psychologist who has a doctoral degree in psychology and at least five years of postgraduate experience in the diagnosis and treatment of emotional and mental disorders, is required to support a finding under this section."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 7827(c), Fam. Code § 7827, subd. (c) (West, current through 2025 legislation) — quoted alongside subdivisions (a) and (e) of the same section 7827; not independent sources of one another (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=7827.)
  "If the rights of a parent are sought to be terminated pursuant to this section, and the parent does not have an attorney, the court shall appoint an attorney for the parent pursuant to Article 4 (commencing with Section 7860) of Chapter 3, whether or not a request for the appointment is made by the parent."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 7827(e), Fam. Code § 7827, subd. (e) (West, current through 2025 legislation) — quoted alongside subdivisions (a) and (c) of the same section 7827; not independent sources of one another (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=7827.)
  Known gap: The two-expert evidentiary requirement is unique to this ground among those described in this document — it does not apply to the abandonment, neglect/dependency, or felony grounds addressed elsewhere. The statute also gives the court discretion to call additional licensed therapists, counselors, or clinical social workers in specified circumstances, and bars calling one who served as the case's adoption service provider; this document does not catalog every such qualification or restriction. The mandatory-counsel provision quoted here applies specifically to this mental-disability ground and cross-references the general counsel-appointment article described in a separate clause of this document.

WHO MAY BRING THE PROCEEDING
Family Code section 7841(a) provides that "an interested person may file a petition under this part for an order or judgment declaring a child free from the custody and control of either or both parents." Subdivision (b) states that, for this purpose, "an 'interested person' is one who has a direct interest in the action, and includes, but is not limited to, a person who has filed, or who intends to file within a period of 6 months, an adoption petition under Section 8714, 8802, or 9000, or a licensed adoption agency to whom the child has been relinquished by the other parent."

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "An interested person may file a petition under this part for an order or judgment declaring a child free from the custody and control of either or both parents."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 7841(a), Fam. Code § 7841, subd. (a) (West, current through 2025 legislation) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=7841.)
  "an “interested person” is one who has a direct interest in the action, and includes, but is not limited to, a person who has filed, or who intends to file within a period of 6 months, an adoption petition under Section 8714, 8802, or 9000, or a licensed adoption agency to whom the child has been relinquished by the other parent."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 7841(b), Fam. Code § 7841, subd. (b) (West, current through 2025 legislation) — quoted alongside subdivision (a) of the same section 7841; not an independent source from it (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=7841.)
  Known gap: The statutory definition of "interested person" is illustrative rather than exhaustive — it expressly "includes, but is not limited to" the listed examples — so the outer boundary of who qualifies as having a sufficient direct interest is left to case-by-case judicial determination that this document does not resolve.

APPOINTMENT OF COUNSEL FOR THE PARENT AND THE CHILD
Family Code section 7860 states that "at the beginning of the proceeding on a petition filed pursuant to this part, counsel shall be appointed as provided in this article," that the public defender or private counsel may serve, and that "the same counsel shall not be appointed to represent both the child and the child's parent." A separate section in the same article, section 7862, provides that "if a parent appears without counsel and is unable to afford counsel, the court shall appoint counsel for the parent, unless that representation is knowingly and intelligently waived."

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "At the beginning of the proceeding on a petition filed pursuant to this part, counsel shall be appointed as provided in this article. The public defender or private counsel may be appointed as counsel pursuant to this article. The same counsel shall not be appointed to represent both the child and the child’s parent."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 7860, Fam. Code § 7860 (West, current through 2025 legislation) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=7860.)
  "If a parent appears without counsel and is unable to afford counsel, the court shall appoint counsel for the parent, unless that representation is knowingly and intelligently waived."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 7862, Fam. Code § 7862 (West, current through 2025 legislation) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=7862.)
  Known gap: Section 7862 does not itself define what makes a waiver of counsel "knowing and intelligent," nor does it or section 7860 specify the indigency standard the court applies in determining inability to afford counsel; both are left to the court's determination in the individual case. Section 7860's appointment mandate and section 7862's indigent-parent entitlement are separate sections within the same Article 4 of Chapter 3 and are not restatements of one another.

THE CHILD'S RIGHT TO BE HEARD AND IN-CHAMBERS TESTIMONY
Family Code section 7891(a) provides that, subject to stated exceptions, "if the child who is the subject of the petition is 10 years of age or older, the child shall be heard by the court in chambers on at least" the child's feelings about the proceeding, the child's feelings about the parent or parents, and the child's custody preference under section 3042. A related section, 7892, separately permits a child's testimony to be taken in chambers and outside a parent's presence where the parent is represented by counsel, counsel is present, and "the testimony of the child may be taken in chambers and outside the presence of the child's parent or parents ... and any of the following circumstances exist" — including that in-chambers testimony is necessary to ensure truthful testimony, that the child is likely to be intimidated by a formal courtroom setting, or that the child is afraid to testify in front of the parent.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "if the child who is the subject of the petition is 10 years of age or older, the child shall be heard by the court in chambers on at least the following matters: (1) The feelings and thoughts of the child concerning the custody proceeding about to take place. (2) The feelings and thoughts of the child about the child’s parent or parents. (3) The child’s preference as to custody, according to Section 3042."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 7891(a), Fam. Code § 7891, subd. (a) (West, current through 2025 legislation) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=7891.)
  "The testimony of the child may be taken in chambers and outside the presence of the child’s parent or parents if the child’s parent or parents are represented by counsel, the counsel is present, and any of the following circumstances exist: (1) The court determines that testimony in chambers is necessary to ensure truthful testimony. (2) The child is likely to be intimidated by a formal courtroom setting. (3) The child is afraid to testify in front of the child’s parent or parents."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 7892(a), Fam. Code § 7892, subd. (a) (West, current through 2025 legislation) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=7892.)
  "A finding pursuant to this section shall be supported by clear and convincing evidence."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 7892(c), Fam. Code § 7892, subd. (c) (West, current through 2025 legislation) — quoted alongside subdivision (a) of the same section 7892; not an independent source from it (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=7892.)
  Known gap: Section 7891's right to be heard applies only to children age 10 or older and does not apply if the child is confined by illness or other incapacity and therefore unable to attend; it also allows the child's counsel to waive the in-chambers hearing. Section 7892's separate in-chambers testimony mechanism applies only in the narrower circumstance where the parent is represented by counsel and that counsel is present, and any finding supporting its use must independently meet the clear-and-convincing-evidence standard stated in that same section — the two sections address related but distinct procedures and are not restatements of each other.

ACKNOWLEDGMENT
By signing below, Jordan Lee acknowledges having reviewed this information sheet regarding the Family Code Part 4 freedom-from-parental-custody-and-control proceeding concerning Alex Lee (date of birth March 14, 2018), potentially involving Pat Morgan, anticipated to be filed in Sacramento County. This information sheet describes the statutory framework only; it is not a petition, does not determine whether any statutory ground applies to particular facts, and is not a substitute for consulting a licensed attorney.

Signed: _________________________ Date: September 1, 2026
Oakland, California

expectedJSON.gap: The two-expert evidentiary requirement is unique to this ground among those described in this document — it does not apply to the abandonment, neglect/dependency, or felony grounds addressed elsewhere. The statute also gives the court discretion to call additional licensed therapists, counselors, or clinical social workers in specified circumstances, and bars calling one who served as the case's adoption service provider; this document does not catalog every such qualification or restriction. The mandatory-counsel provision quoted here applies specifically to this mental-disability ground and cross-references the general counsel-appointment article described in a separate clause of this document.

expectedJSON.body: Family Code section 7841(a) provides that "an interested person may file a petition under this part for an order or judgment declaring a child free from the custody and control of either or both parents." Subdivision (b) states that, for this purpose, "an 'interested person' is one who has a direct interest in the action, and includes, but is not limited to, a person who has filed, or who intends to file within a period of 6 months, an adoption petition under Section 8714, 8802, or 9000, or a licensed adoption agency to whom the child has been relinquished by the other parent."

citations.cite: Fam. Code § 7841, subd. (a) (West, current through 2025 legislation)
citations.quote: An interested person may file a petition under this part for an order or judgment declaring a child free from the custody and control of either or both parents.

citations.cite: Fam. Code § 7841, subd. (b) (West, current through 2025 legislation) — quoted alongside subdivision (a) of the same section 7841; not an independent source from it
citations.quote: an “interested person” is one who has a direct interest in the action, and includes, but is not limited to, a person who has filed, or who intends to file within a period of 6 months, an adoption petition under Section 8714, 8802, or 9000, or a licensed adoption agency to whom the child has been relinquished by the other parent.

expectedJSON.gap: The statutory definition of "interested person" is illustrative rather than exhaustive — it expressly "includes, but is not limited to" the listed examples — so the outer boundary of who qualifies as having a sufficient direct interest is left to case-by-case judicial determination that this document does not resolve.

expectedJSON.body: Family Code section 7860 states that "at the beginning of the proceeding on a petition filed pursuant to this part, counsel shall be appointed as provided in this article," that the public defender or private counsel may serve, and that "the same counsel shall not be appointed to represent both the child and the child's parent." A separate section in the same article, section 7862, provides that "if a parent appears without counsel and is unable to afford counsel, the court shall appoint counsel for the parent, unless that representation is knowingly and intelligently waived."

citations.quote: At the beginning of the proceeding on a petition filed pursuant to this part, counsel shall be appointed as provided in this article. The public defender or private counsel may be appointed as counsel pursuant to this article. The same counsel shall not be appointed to represent both the child and the child’s parent.
If a parent appears without counsel and is unable to afford counsel, the court shall appoint counsel for the parent, unless that representation is knowingly and intelligently waived.

expectedJSON.gap: Section 7862 does not itself define what makes a waiver of counsel "knowing and intelligent," nor does it or section 7860 specify the indigency standard the court applies in determining inability to afford counsel; both are left to the court's determination in the individual case. Section 7860's appointment mandate and section 7862's indigent-parent entitlement are separate sections within the same Article 4 of Chapter 3 and are not restatements of one another.

expectedJSON.body: Family Code section 7891(a) provides that, subject to stated exceptions, "if the child who is the subject of the petition is 10 years of age or older, the child shall be heard by the court in chambers on at least" the child's feelings about the proceeding, the child's feelings about the parent or parents, and the child's custody preference under section 3042. A related section, 7892, separately permits a child's testimony to be taken in chambers and outside a parent's presence where the parent is represented by counsel, counsel is present, and "the testimony of the child may be taken in chambers and outside the presence of the child's parent or parents ... and any of the following circumstances exist" — including that in-chambers testimony is necessary to ensure truthful testimony, that the child is likely to be intimidated by a formal courtroom setting, or that the child is afraid to testify in front of the parent.

citations.cite: Fam. Code § 7891, subd. (a) (West, current through 2025 legislation)
citations.quote: if the child who is the subject of the petition is 10 years of age or older, the child shall be heard by the court in chambers on at least the following matters: (1) The feelings and thoughts of the child concerning the custody proceeding about to take place. (2) The feelings and thoughts of the child about the child’s parent or parents. (3) The child’s preference as to custody, according to Section 3042.

citations.cite: Fam. Code § 7892, subd. (a) (West, current through 2025 legislation)
citations.quote: The testimony of the child may be taken in chambers and outside the presence of the child’s parent or parents if the child’s parent or parents are represented by counsel, the counsel is present, and any of the following circumstances exist: (1) The court determines that testimony in chambers is necessary to ensure truthful testimony. (2) The child is likely to be intimidated by a formal courtroom setting. (3) The child is afraid to testify in front of the child’s parent or parents.

citations.cite: Fam. Code § 7892, subd. (c) (West, current through 2025 legislation) — quoted alongside subdivision (a) of the same section 7892; not an independent source from it
citations.quote: A finding pursuant to this section shall be supported by clear and convincing evidence.

expectedJSON.gap: Section 7891's right to be heard applies only to children age 10 or older and does not apply if the child is confined by illness or other incapacity and therefore unable to attend; it also allows the child's counsel to waive the in-chambers hearing. Section 7892's separate in-chambers testimony mechanism applies only in the narrower circumstance where the parent is represented by counsel and that counsel is present, and any finding supporting its use must independently meet the clear-and-convincing-evidence standard stated in that same section — the two sections address related but distinct procedures and are not restatements of each other.
